lens: What does this circuit test, teach and expose about the vehicle model? Weights: coverage 30, diagnostic legibility 25, honest #137 exposure 15, regression value 20, M6 determinism/ghost 10.

scores.strongest: Diagnostic legibility. It is the only one of the four whose corner-speed claims survived independent recomputation: the verifier reproduced 12 of the 13 quoted lock ceilings to within 0.1 km/h straight from drive_probe.gd's three 0.25-lock rows (T1 148.41 vs 148.4, T3 67.49 vs 67.5 and 53.50 vs 53.5, T6b 86.20 vs 86.2 and 53.80 vs 53.8, T7 109.48 vs 109.4, T8b 138.54 vs 138.6 and 118.98 vs 119.0, T2 292.5 vs 292.6). It is also the only layout using the correct geometric line formula R + e(1+k)/(k-1), e=(W-1.4)/2, k=sec(theta/2) - the same closed form racecraft's verifier derived independently - rather than an inside-edge offset.
scores.weakest: Coverage of the named tickets. Zero mentions of #139 and #39, one mention each of #38 and #40, no caster jacking, no surface transition. T2 is 0.78 g on a 186.0 m line radius with a 292.6 km/h lock ceiling - the author calls it 'one bureaucrat' and that is accurate: 45 deg of the lap tests nothing at all. And the reverse layout's central geometry claim is false - vertical curvature is invariant under s -> L-s, so the 847.4/627.8/728.5/767.7/317.6/627.5 m 'reverse minima' obtained by swapping K=15 and K=20 are not a test; under the correct test VC2 (concave, R=900 m) sits inside the 41.5 m reverse braking zone at ~138 km/h needing 952.2 m.
scores.reasoning: Coverage 23/30: the gearbox coverage is the deepest and the only checkable one - 35 gear references, an explicit per-corner gear table that the verifier confirmed against gearbox.h exactly (85 km/h in 3rd = 13,270 rpm, 4th spans 70.5-109.6 km/h, 143.9 km/h = 13,865 rpm in 6th), T3 as the only 1st-gear corner with five downshifts in a 45.0 m zone and five upshifts up 186.7 m of 5% climb, T7 as the only 3rd-gear corner. All six gears are located by corner, which no other proposal does. It is also the only layout whose primary overtaking mechanism is derived from the tire model rather than from asphalt width: T1's friction-ellipse arithmetic gives the pinned defender 0.367 of longitudinal headroom against the attacker's 0.665 over 99.484 m of arc, so combined slip is the thing under test. T4's braking zone (11.8 m, 120.8 to 100 km/h) deliberately opens inside the last 30 m of a 1,300 m convex run-out, which is a normal-load-during-braking test with a stated cause. The T4-T5 esse has an analytic falsifiable answer: 32.470 m between opposite hands, a full 9.5 m crossing needs 3.07 g and the kart has 1.86, so both corners must be driven from mid-track. #32 gets 2.98 s of constant-radius left at T1, and the verifier found three MORE corners over 2.5 s (T8b 3.373 s, T6 3.142 s, T3 2.791 s) than the document claimed, which is under-claimed coverage rather than over-claimed. Against that: nothing tests curb strikes at speed by name, nothing tests engine braking shaping entry, nothing tests a surface transition, and caster jacking is never mentioned. Legibility 22/25: the sector design is the only one in the four written as a diagnostic partition - sector 2 is named as the gearbox sector on the evidence of 11 shifts against 2 in sector 1, and the rationale says outright that 'a sector-2 delta means the hairpin exit or the esse, and those are distinguishable by where the driver was in the gearbox'. Every corner publishes grip ceiling AND lock ceiling AND margin, free-line and pinned-line separately. The verifier's hits are mostly bookkeeping: 0.586 s of sector sum unaccounted, 12,300 rpm where gearbox.h gives 13,737, an invented 18.4 m separation where the real figure is 152.645 m, a 355 m reused from an unrelated hypothetical. One is substantive - T4's esse 'ceiling drops to 100.0 km/h, no margin' is the GRIP ceiling; the lock ceiling is 94.88 km/h, and that is the number carrying the conclusion. #137 11/15: one deliberate exposure (T6b pinned at 22.0 m, lock ceiling 53.8 km/h against a 64 km/h apex, 10.2 km/h over) plus a graduated ladder of thin margins on the defensive line - T3 defensive 1.5 km/h, T5 esse 2.3 km/h, T8b pinned 3.0 km/h. That is a raceable balance and it is the brief's own preferred one. But a good driver on a good line never meets the cliff here, so the defect can be driven around for 25 laps, which is a partial hide. Regression 18/20: the per-corner margin ladder (18.7 / 22.2 / 24.4 / 12.2 / 2.3 / 10.5 / 3.0 / 1.5 km/h) is literally a sensitivity ordering - a grip or lock regression breaks T5 first, then T8b pinned, then T3's defensive line, and the sector it lands in names the corner. Three sectors within 1.0 s of each other (15.049 / 16.048 / 15.398) with distinct dominant subsystems. And it is the only document that refused to publish reverse sector times off a forward pass, on the stated grounds that it 'would be exactly the kind of model-not-measurement conclusion this project has been bitten by'. M6 8/10: elevation closes to -5.98e-06 m, plan closure 0.478 mm, one elevation profile, vertical curves at 1.3-2.5x minimum by explicit policy rather than at the floor, and 300 m of the lap (T2 and the shelf) where nothing can bifurcate. Deduction is the reverse first corner: T8 reversed is a 130 deg decreasing-radius right entered 77.2 m after the start line at a claimed 132 km/h that the verifier puts 15+ km/h optimistic (widest single arc 58.06 m = 2.362 g, grip ceiling 117.1 km/h) - a bifurcation immediately after the line is the worst place for one in a ghost.

scores.strongest: Coverage breadth, by a distance. It is the only one of the four that names #139 (7 hits), #39 (4), #40 (4), caster jacking (3) and a surface transition (11), and the only one with a back-to-back left/right matched pair for the 2.43 g vs 2.81 g asymmetry: T4 Le Esse, two 50 m / 28 deg arcs of identical radius and identical kerb 0.9 s apart at 112.4 km/h. That comparison is the one claim in the whole proposal that is robust to the line-model defect, because both halves inherit the same systematic error.
scores.weakest: The radius ladder - the thesis - is built on the wrong line. Every racing-line radius in the document is exactly Rc + W/2 - 0.7 m, verified on all twelve corner segments, i.e. the hug-the-inside-edge path with no dependence on direction change or on the adjacent straights. Recomputing the minimum-curvature line gives T2 94.3 m not 34.3 (2.75x), T6 50.6 m not 23.3 (2.17x), T10 128.1 m not 42.8 (2.99x), T7 54.5 m not 28.8 (1.89x), T8 283.9 m not 114.3 (2.48x). T2 Il Quarto is sold as sitting 1.7 m outside the sweep's 32.64 m quarter-lock row and is probably a 60-90 m corner; T6 La Vite is sold as the low-g / high-lock CONTROL for the caster-jacking reading and on a 50.6 m line is a fast corner at low lock, which destroys the T2/T6 pairing outright.
scores.reasoning: Coverage 25/30: on intent this is the best coverage document any of the four produced, and it is the only one that treats the vehicle model as a checklist with a corner per item. T3 Il Curvone gives #32 the longest steady state in the set - 130.9 m of arc, 4.17 s at 112.9 km/h on a 54.8 m line, left-handed against the 2.43 g threshold. T8 Il Ciglio is the only purpose-built #139 fixture in four proposals: a 30 mm vertical-faced kerb, 40 m of it, met at 120.7-132.2 km/h once a lap and 25 times in a Final, which is also the repeated-crossing cost measurement the ticket still owes. T5 Il Frantoio puts 2.51 s on the 2nd/3rd shift boundary so auto-shift has to make a decision the driver can argue with (#40). T7 La Staccatina needs 14.0 m of braking from 102.9 km/h, so the entry is set by lifting in 2nd and the pedal is a correction (#39) - the only corner in the set whose entry can be got wrong without touching the brake. T9 gives #38 the slowest point in the set (49.6 km/h) with 126.2 m of +2.8% climb to pay for a bogged exit. T10 carries the only authored surface transition - a resurfacing joint 8 m before turn-in so the grip step lands under an already-threshold pedal. T1 is the only deliberate combined-braking-and-turning corner, decreasing radius 66 -> 32 m with 26.1 m of braking that runs out at turn-in. Six gears covered (6th at T8, 1st or 2nd at T9). I dock 5 because roughly four of those ten provocations - T2's #137 boundary, T6's caster control, T7's #39 lift-entry, and part of T8's kerb argument - depend on radii the verifier showed are 1.9x to 2.8x too small. Legibility 20/25: structurally the best - one named question per corner is the stated design rule, cliff_relation is a published per-corner field with three values, and T2 vs T5 vs T9 deliberately separate 'can you stay the right side of the boundary' from 'what does the gearbox do once past it' from 'the cliff proper'. Against that, T5 combines gearbox + past-cliff + a -3.6% exit descent, and 11 of the 13 vertical curves sit on a corner boundary (T5's turn-in under threshold braking at 0.6 m, T9's turn-in at the end of the biggest braking zone, T6's turn-in at 2.0 m), which puts a vertical-load transient on top of eleven of the readings the layout exists to take. #137 12/15: the most sophisticated treatment in the set and the most honest ratio - one on the boundary, three past it, six safe, with T2 and T5 explicitly separated by what they ask. The risk is that the line model may collapse the real exposure to T9 (20.3 m, hard-bounded, robust) and T5 (25.8 -> 34.8 m, only 1.35x off) and delete T2 and T6 entirely. Regression 16/20: 49.44 s with most corners on the safe side makes lap time stable and interpretable rather than chaotic, and sector 3's rationale - 'a sector delta here reads as a single question: did you get the hairpin right' - is the right shape. Deducted because two of the three sector questions rest on the corners whose radii are unvalidated, and because the layout has only two braking zones over 20 m forward (26.1 m at T1, 39.4 m at T9), so a braking-model regression has almost nothing to move. M6 7/10: three past-cliff corners (T5, T6, T9) are scrub-region bifurcations, but all three are slow (49-64 km/h) which limits amplification. The real hazard is T1 - a compound with the brake still on at 1.4 g lateral at 135.9 km/h entry, the first corner of the lap, judged cold. A ghost that diverges there diverges before anything else has happened. Separately, the S/F straight sits 20.558 m in plan and 8.094 m vertically from the T7 approach - a 76.7% face over roughly 60 m of each - which is a construction and mesh problem rather than a determinism one, but it is a real violation the author flagged in risks and then reported as passing.

scores.strongest: It found a coverage axis the other three missed entirely, and it found it incidentally, from the terrain lens rather than from a checklist. The derivation that the CIK vertical-radius rule is exactly a speed-independent cap on vertical acceleration - a = K/12.96, so 0.157 g concave and 0.118 g convex at any speed whatsoever, +27.5 kgf and -20.7 kgf on a 175 kg kart - turns gradient into a quantified normal-load input with an analytic expected value. T6's exit compression (-0.50% to +7.81% at 118 km/h, 58 m at the legal minimum) squashes the kart into the road exactly as traction sets the speed for the next 132 m; T7's crest takes 11.8% off the driven axle at the apex of a locked-axle hairpin. Nothing in the other three proposals tests tire load sensitivity with a number attached.
scores.weakest: Three fast corners solved backwards to the grip ceiling. On the author's own design line T1, T3 and T5 land at 1.848, 1.854 and 1.860 g - 99.4%, 99.7% and 100.0% of the measured 1.86 g. On the centerline five of seven corners exceed the ceiling outright (T1 2.026 g, T3 1.983, T5 1.983, T4 1.937, T6 1.916). And the sweep's largest measured row is 58.49 m, so T1 (60.3 m), T3 (66.3 m) and T5 (69.3 m) are all extrapolations past the largest radius the project has ever measured.
scores.reasoning: Coverage 20/30: the normal-load axis is real, novel and worth 8 points on its own, and the blind-crest sight-time derivation (a 1.79 s floor that depends only on K and driver eye height, with the two built crests measuring 1.86 s and 1.97 s) is a genuine camera/AI/LOD input nobody else produced. #32 gets T5, 79 m of left at building load to 1.86 g at the exit, 2.2 s, 1.31x margin - shorter than instrument's 4.17 s and rhythm's 2.98 s but adequate. #137 gets three visits. Against that the ticket coverage is the thinnest in the set: zero mentions of #38, #39, #40 or #139, no caster jacking, one mention of 'surface', and a gear treatment that goes no deeper than 'down to 1st or 2nd'. Three of the four M3b feel tickets are simply absent. Legibility 10/25: this is where it falls apart. T7 Il Ciglione is deliberately five things at once - past the #137 cliff at a 22.8 m line, 0.118 g light over a crest, blind with 31 m of sight at turn-in, uphill braking at 1.61 g effective, on a locked axle - which is precisely the brief's own anti-pattern, 'a corner that combines four things tests nothing'. When the kart misbehaves there, no subsystem is identifiable. The three-corners-at-the-ceiling problem compounds it: a tire-model change moves T1, T3 and T5 together, so the lap time is one binary amplified three times rather than three separable readings. And the arithmetic is not reliable - La Conca's braking recomputes to 8.79 m against the stated 3.8 m, a 2.3x error that flips the stated +1.5 m margin to -3.48 m of overlap with the compression's vertical curve. #137 11/15: T7 is the best-argued single #137 corner in the four, precisely because it refuses to repeat the test track - 'it is deliberately NOT at 11 m: the test track already has the corner that walks into the cliff and stops. This one asks the driver to find the last few degrees of lock that still pay.' And T4's reasoning that 14 m of width is a #137 mitigation (at 8 m the same 26 m centerline gives a 29.3 m line and lands the wrong side of quarter lock) is the most useful method in any of the four documents. Docked because T7's exposure is unreadable for the reason above. Regression 10/20: high sensitivity, poorly localized. Every vertical curve is at exactly R = V^2/K by explicit policy - recomputed vertical accelerations 0.1180 g and 0.1574 g, the legal maxima to four decimals - and five of six sit in a section art 7.2 names (T3's braking zone by 3.48 m, T5's arc by 2.73 m, T7's arc entirely, 9.02 m in each half). And half the regression target does not exist: the reverse layout is illegal, with the two Il Salto vertical curves overlapping by 13.21 m driven backwards (44.20 m of half-lengths against 30.98 m of road, robust down to 4.06 m even at a conservative 120 km/h), and the T2-reversed braking zone still overlapping a minimum-radius curve by 8.92 m - the exact defect the author claims to have fixed. M6 4/10: the worst ghost target of the four. Three corners at 100% of the grip ceiling, two compressions at exactly the maximum legal vertical acceleration sitting inside braking zones, and a past-cliff blind hairpin. A replay that diverges at T3 could be the compression, the ceiling or the line, and there is no way to tell them apart from the trace.

scores.strongest: Two things. First, T4 The Cellar is the one genuinely hard-bounded #137 visit in the set: a 16 m centerline in a 10 m road gives a 19.56 m widest line against the sweep's 18.99 m / 0.88 g / 46.0 km/h row, and the verifier's independent geometric optimum is 21.46 m - the only corner in four proposals where the corridor itself forces the radius and the claim survives a proper line solve. Second, its 14.5872 m of elevation range - the largest of the four - buys the best braking geometry anywhere in the set: T4 reversed is 111.75 m of -4.38% descent to 143.7 km/h, the kart's only visit to its own top speed in either direction of any layout, into a 48.5 m braking zone.
scores.weakest: Four of nine corners are not the corners the document says they are, and each error runs the same direction - toward making the layout sound like it tests more than it does. T5's apex is stated as 143.9 km/h between a 116.5 entry and a 125.4 exit, on a +4.38% climb, which needs 5.86 m/s2 of net acceleration on a gradient that costs 0.43 - and the same corner's prose says 'taken flat at 116-126' while the document's own measured block says the forward top speed is 137.8. T6 is claimed at 119.1 km/h and 1.86 g with an 8.4 m braking zone; its geometric maximum line radius is 121.56 m, 1.86 g there is 169.5 km/h, so it is flat out and the independent profile takes it at 133.2 km/h with no braking event at all. T7 is claimed at 94.2 km/h - 'deliberately slow so the field concertinas' - against a computed 107-109 km/h, and that concertina is the premise of the primary overtaking argument.
scores.reasoning: Coverage 15/30: the narrowest of the four and the only one that deliberately declines a test it could have had - T3's kerb is specified low-profile 30 mm explicitly because 'at 130 km/h in a left-hander at 1.86 g a normal 50 mm kerb would be a rollover trigger', which is a defensible circuit decision and a refusal of the #139 case. Zero mentions of #139, #39, caster jacking or surface transitions; one mention each of #38 and #40, both hung on T4. First gear is never used anywhere on the lap (T4 is 6th to 2nd). What it does cover it covers well: T3 gives #32 a 95 deg left at the ceiling, and the verifier's independent line (78.24 m against the claimed 71.76) only moves it to 1.71 g, so the corner survives as the lap's biggest sustained left; the exposure is actually 3.29 s rather than the stated 2.52 s, because the stated figure divides centerline arc by racing-line speed. T2's decreasing-radius exit under power on a locked axle is a real traction test. Legibility 8/25: the lowest score I gave anything. Beyond the four wrong corners, the defensive-line arithmetic that carries the entire racing thesis is wrong by 2x to 30x - T1 claimed 27 m at 66.7 km/h against a measured inner-half line of 51.50 m (110.3 km/h), T6 claimed 26.5 m against 73.53 m, T7 claimed 24 m against 36.49 m - and at T1 the correctly computed pinned line (51.50 m) is LARGER than the author's own free line (48.85 m), which in the document's own frame makes the defender faster than the attacker. A developer debugging a physics anomaly against this document would be misdirected at four of nine corners. #137 8/15: the intent is the most honest of the four - the layout says outright that its central mechanic is a consequence of an open defect and that 'every number in this document should be re-measured the day #137 closes'. But the mechanism is computed on radii that are not the radii, so of the five claimed cliff interactions only T4 is real. Regression 10/20: the lap is the shortest in time (42.918 claimed, 39.731 independent, 7.4% apart) and the sectors are reported as exactly 14.306 s each, three times, summing to the lap time to four decimals at boundaries round to the half-metre - three independent integrations of a speed profile do not land on the same millisecond, and the independent pass gives 12.764 / 13.422 / 13.546. A sector split that is a derivation presented as a measurement cannot be a regression signal. M6 4/10: the document publishes TWO elevation profiles that describe different roads. The segment-grade list closes to -5.116e-05 m over a 14.5872 m range; integrating the eight published vertical curves at their published stations gives +0.601189 m of closure error over a 12.6240 m range, and the two disagree by up to 2.0947 m. Build the ribbon from one and the ghost reference from the other and you get replay divergence with no cause visible anywhere in the simulation - which is exactly the failure mode this criterion exists to screen for.

best_corners: instrument / T4 Le Esse: two 50 m arcs of 28 deg, opposite hands, identical 25 mm kerbs, 0.9 s apart at 112.4 km/h and 1.82 g. It is the only test in four proposals for the 2.43 g vs 2.81 g rollover asymmetry that a driver can actually resolve, and it is the only claim in the instrument document that is immune to its own line-model defect, because both halves inherit the same systematic error and the reading is a ratio. Graft: replace rhythm's T4-T5 esse's mismatched 30 m / 34 m pair with a matched pair at one radius, so the same 32.5 m link tests the lateral transient AND the asymmetry instead of only the transient. Author it explicitly as a matched pair in track.json so a later radius tweak to one half is caught.

instrument / T8 Il Ciglio: a 30 mm vertical-faced kerb, 40 m of it, on a 34 deg / 110 m corner taken flat from 120.7 to 132.2 km/h. The only purpose-built #139 fixture in the set - a curb a driver cannot avoid above 120 km/h, struck once a lap and 25 times in a Final, which is also the repeated-crossing cost figure #139 still owes. Graft onto rhythm's T2 Il Filo, which is currently 0.78 g on a 186 m line and admitted filler: give its flush 40 mm kerb a vertical face and the corner stops being a bureaucrat and becomes the fastest kerb contact on the property at 136 km/h. Keep the corner's grip demand at 0.78 g so the reading stays a pure kerb reading.

instrument / T10 La Cesta's resurfacing joint: a grip step across the road 8 m before turn-in, so the transition arrives after the pedal is already at threshold rather than before it. The only authored surface transition in four proposals, and art 12's paint ban does not reach it. Graft into rhythm's T3 braking zone - 45.0 m from 141.3 km/h is the deepest zone in the set and the only one with room to separate the step from the initial application. Do NOT graft it into a short zone; instrument's own 11.9 m at T10 is too thin to read.

instrument / T5 Il Frantoio and T7 La Staccatina as a pair: T5 holds 64.3 km/h for 2.51 s on the 2nd/3rd shift boundary so auto-shift has to make a decision the driver can argue with (#40); T7 needs only 14.0 m of braking from 102.9 km/h, so the entry is set by lifting in 2nd and the pedal is a correction (#39). These are the only two corners in four proposals built for those tickets. Graft both into rhythm's sector 2, which already owns the gearbox (11 shifts against 2 in sector 1) - the shift-boundary corner belongs on the 186.7 m climb's exit and the lift-entry corner belongs where a short zone is already forced.

instrument / T1 Curva del Banco: 26.1 m of braking from 135.9 km/h that runs out exactly at turn-in, then the radius halves 66 -> 32 m, so the brake is still on at 1.4 g of lateral - and it is corner one, judged cold. The only deliberate combined-braking-and-turning load-transfer corner in the set. Graft as the entry half of whichever layout's first corner, and re-derive the radii from a proper minimum-curvature line before believing the 1.4 g.

rhythm / T4-T5 esse: 32.470 m between opposite-hand corners where crossing the usable 9.5 m demands 3.07 g and the kart has 1.86, so the driver gets about 3.10 m of movement and both corners must be driven from mid-track. Analytic, falsifiable and it costs a measurable 0.64 s against the same radii in isolation. Keep it in whatever wins; it is the cheapest lateral-transient test in the set and the only one with a closed-form expected answer.

rhythm / T1 Ronda's friction-ellipse overtaking argument: 99.484 m of 12 m wide constant radius where the pinned defender runs 65.3 m at 1.73 g with 0.367 of longitudinal headroom against the attacker's 81.4 m at 1.39 g and 0.665, so the attacker has 1.8x the available drive for the whole arc. The only overtaking mechanism in four proposals derived from the tire model rather than from asphalt width, and therefore the only one that would still be a valid test after #137 closes. Graft the method, not just the corner: any wide long corner can carry it.

terrain / the ramp-foot compression at T6's exit: -0.50% to +7.81% at 118 km/h, 58 m of vertical curve, +0.157 g and +27.5 kgf on a 175 kg kart, landing where traction sets the speed for the next 132 m. The only normal-load-modulation test in the set and the only one with a speed-independent analytic answer (a = K/12.96, so 0.157 g concave and 0.118 g convex at any speed). Graft into a slow section where the vertical radius fits cheaply, and keep it OUT of a braking zone and out of an arc - terrain's own version violates art 7.2 and is unreadable for it. Placed clean, it is a load-sensitivity probe with an expected value.

terrain / T4's width-as-a-#137-control method: 14 m of width holds the design line at 32.3 m, essentially the sweep's 32.64 m row exactly; at the 8 m regulation floor the same 26 m centerline gives 29.3 m and falls the wrong side of quarter lock. This is the cheapest way to move a corner onto or off the cliff without touching the plan geometry, and it is the single most useful piece of method in any of the four documents. Adopt it as the convention for authoring any corner whose cliff_relation is load-bearing.

racecraft / T4 The Cellar driven in reverse: 111.75 m of -4.38% descent to 143.7 km/h - the only place any of the four layouts reaches the kart's measured top speed in either direction - into a 48.5 m braking zone and out onto 319 m of climbing full throttle. The strongest single argument in the set for reverse being content rather than a mirror, and the only braking zone long enough to be a real braking-model regression signal. It needs racecraft's 14.6 m of elevation range to exist; rhythm's 7.4 m and instrument's 8.5 m cannot produce it. Worth taking the elevation budget up for.
concerns: The brief prescribes a CENTERLINE walk and then asks every proposal for apex speeds, sustained g and a cliff_relation - all of which are racing-line quantities - and never specifies a racing-line convention. Four agents used four: instrument Rc + W/2 - 0.7 (the inside edge), terrain Rc + (W-1.4)/2, rhythm R + e(1+k)/(k-1) with e=(W-1.4)/2 and k=sec(theta/2), racecraft a geometric optimum capped at 2x Rc. On the same corner these differ by up to 3x (instrument's T10: 42.8 m against a computed 128.1 m). This is the single largest source of incomparability between the four proposals and it is the brief's omission, not the agents'. Name the formula - rhythm's is the one two independent verifiers converged on - and the comparison becomes real.

The separation rule is stated as a constant when it is width-dependent: '6 m of clear ground... with 8 m width that is >= 14 m between centerlines'. Every one of the four layouts is wider than 8 m somewhere, because the brief itself says widening is free plausibility. At instrument's 14 m hairpin the same 6 m rule needs 20 m between centerlines. Any validation pass that hardcodes 14 m - which is what Part 4 asks all four to compute - passes an illegal layout wherever the road is wide.

The separation check is purely horizontal, so it silently passes a cliff. Instrument's start/finish straight sits 20.558 m from the T7 approach in plan and 8.094 m below it - a 76.7% face over roughly 60 m of each - and it passes the brief's check by 6.5 m. No verge, no run-off and no non-negative-slope requirement can be met there. A vertical-separation rule needs to exist alongside the plan one, and it is written down nowhere in the brief, ARCHITECTURE section 11 or REFERENCES.md.

The steering-lock sweep confounds lock with throttle. The three 0.25-lock rows are at throttle 0.30, 0.60 and 1.00, so 'the quarter-lock ceiling at radius r' - a quantity every one of the four documents interpolates dozens of times, and the quantity the entire #137 vocabulary rests on - is read off a curve that is not a function of radius alone. Rhythm flagged this as its own largest error source and it is correct. Until drive_probe.gd sweeps lock at fixed throttle, every cliff_relation in every proposal is provisional.

Part 4's elevation gate does not ask for the vertical-radius check to be run in the REVERSE direction, and reverse is a first-class layout per ADR-0046 and GAMEDESIGN section 10. R = V^2/K is speed-dependent and speed is direction-dependent, so a profile legal forward can be illegal backwards. Terrain's reverse layout is illegal by 13.21 m of vertical-curve overlap for exactly this reason, and rhythm got the correction backwards (it swapped K=15 and K=20 on reversal; vertical curvature is invariant under s -> L-s, so a crest is a crest either way and only the speed changes). Two of four got this wrong in opposite directions. It belongs in the gate.

The brief builds every overtaking argument on a tow - 'a long enough straight for a tow' is item (a) of its own three-part definition - and there is no slipstream model in the simulation. Racecraft flagged it. Every tow_length_m in four documents describes an effect the sim does not currently have, which means the two-overtaking-spots requirement cannot be validated by driving until it does.

Two headline vehicle numbers are internally inconsistent and the brief propagates both. 'Best sustained lateral 1.86 g' against the lock sweep's own best row of 1.84 g - which moves a 55 m corner's apex by about 0.7 km/h and matters because three of terrain's corners are designed to 99.4-100.0% of whichever number is right. And the 143.9 km/h top speed the vertical-radius table is worked against is a speed no Grade 1 circuit can produce, because the 200 m straight cap binds first: the fastest point in any of the four layouts is 141.3 km/h and most are 136-138. The table is conservative by roughly 15%, which is the safe direction, but the operative design speed should be stated.

The brief quotes 0-100 km/h in 4.50 s as a kart property while noting it is issue #121, 'all launch'. Every lap-time estimate in all four proposals inherits it, and it moves the first lap of a race far more than a flying lap - which is the lap the 8-kart session runner actually starts with and the one the grid is judged on.

Minor and worth reconciling: the brief's vertical-radius table gives 331 m for the 81.3 km/h concave case where REFERENCES.md gives 330 (81.3^2/20 = 330.5). The brief rounded up where the sourced document rounded down, and REFERENCES.md is the binding one.

Four agents wrote into one shared scratchpad with generic filenames, and instrument reported that a module it had read and was importing (design.py) belonged to another agent and could have changed underneath it mid-run. CLAUDE.md's worktree rule exists for exactly this and does not currently extend to the scratchpad. Every fan-out brief should name a private subdirectory.
summary: Rhythm 82, instrument 80, terrain 55, racecraft 45. Correcting for the instrument's home-field advantage as instructed did not change the top two much - it changed which of them I would build. Instrument has the widest coverage in the set by a clear margin and it is the only layout that touches #139, #39, #40, caster jacking, a surface transition and a back-to-back left/right rollover pair, all of which it achieved deliberately. But its coverage is delivered through a radius ladder whose racing-line model is the hug-the-inside-edge path - Rc + W/2 - 0.7 on all twelve corner segments, verified - and recomputing the minimum-curvature line moves the small-radius rungs by 1.9x to 3.0x, which is exactly where the #137 and caster-jacking claims live. Rhythm achieved less coverage but achieved it incidentally and, more importantly, achieved it CHECKABLY: it is the only proposal whose corner-speed claims survived independent recomputation (12 of 13 lock ceilings reproduced to 0.1 km/h from the raw sweep rows), the only one using the geometric line formula two independent verifiers derived, the only one that publishes a per-corner margin ladder that doubles as a regression sensitivity ordering, and the only one whose sectors are written as diagnostic partitions with a named dominant subsystem each. Under a lens that asks 'when the kart does something wrong, can a developer tell which subsystem did it', that wins. Terrain contributed the one genuinely new coverage axis in the whole exercise - gradient as a quantified normal-load input, with the speed-independent 0.157 g / 0.118 g cap falling out of the regulation - and then made it unreadable by building T7 as five simultaneous tests and solving three fast corners backwards to 100.0% of the grip ceiling. Racecraft is last on this lens and it is not close: four of its nine corners are not the corners it says they are, its defensive-line radii are 2x to 30x wrong in a way that makes the defender faster than the attacker in its own frame, and it publishes two elevation profiles that disagree by 2.09 m - which is a replay-divergence source with no cause visible in the sim, the specific failure this criterion screens for. The build I would recommend is rhythm's chassis with instrument's coverage grafted on: keep rhythm's line model, margin ladder, sector partition, gear map and T4-T5 esse; import instrument's Le Esse matched pair, the T8 kerb as a #139 fixture on rhythm's currently-empty T2, the T10 resurfacing joint into rhythm's 45 m hairpin zone, and the T5/T7 gearbox-and-engine-braking pair into rhythm's sector 2; take terrain's ramp-foot compression and its width-as-a-#137-control method; and raise the elevation budget toward racecraft's 14.6 m so a reversed downhill 48 m braking zone becomes available, because none of the top two can currently produce one.
